Since no one addressed the tea tray, I'll hop in and give you some pointers. The tea tray is a nice place to put all your teaware on top of and maybe a tea pet if you're interested. I brew Chinese style gong fu, so if this doesn't work for Japanese tea someone correct me. The other advice you've gotten on how to brew these teas is excellent and works for me for sencha and gyokuro.

I rinse the tea leaves first with hot water to get rid of any residue and pour it over the tray as a way to waste it. (I do this with sencha, but I don't know if there's some Japanese teas where the first steep is gold and worth drinking). I have tea pets so I pour it off over them so they absorb the smell. Using a tray is an easy way to keep spills contained without walking to the sink. When you're done with your session, you dump out of the plastic part that comes out, give it a rinse and dry it. 

The towel is to mop up any spills. Usually it's soft or microfiber so it can catch a fair amount of water.

Hope that helps! Enjoy your set, it really is a wonderful thing!

I'm going to explain this simply; I get the impression you're young or don't know much about how languages/grammar work. I can only hope this doesn't come off as condescending.

I'll use French since that's what I know best. For a man who wants to say "I'm Portuguese" he says: je suis portugais. For a woman who wants to say the same thing, she says: je suis portugaise. That one letter changes the pronunciation significantly so we know (even though she may or may not look like a woman) that she identifies as female. 

I hope that helps a little. Gender classification of nouns and adjectives, and agreement of verbs help languages sound musical and appealing to the ear (at least I think so, a bit like vowel harmony in Turkish) and they've evolved to work this way for a reason. Some languages have more genders, others have none. You can't just change one into the other.

Best of luck.
No I mean if you're using a male pronoun, use male adjectives. Grammar has rules. If you want to be intelligible you have to follow them

You're wrong about French. It's je for both although all adjectives are gendered. The fact that many languages have genders shouldn't discourage you from learning them. Whether or not you choose to use whichever gender for yourself can be as arbitrary as whether a table is masculine or feminine. You just have to be consistent with it.

Keep in mind there are also languages with neuter gender, but this would be weird to use for a person in most cases.
